theme: simple harmonic motion of a particle
enonce_markdown: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion along a straight line with amplitude $0.5\ \mathrm m$ and period $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\ \mathrm s$. The greatest magnitude of its acceleration, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For simple harmonic motion $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, the acceleration is $-\omega^{2}x$, so its greatest magnitude (at the ends of the oscillation, $x=\pm a$) is $\omega^{2}a$.

### Solution

$$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{2\pi/3}=3\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\qquad |\ddot x|_{\max}=\omega^{2}a=9(0.5)=4.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$

**Answer: c.** The value $1.5$ is the greatest speed $\omega a$, $3$ is just $\omega$, and $9$ is $\omega^{2}$ without the amplitude.

theme: simple harmonic motion of a particle
enonce_markdown: The displacement of a particle from a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds is $x = 0.4\cos 5t$ metres. The speed of the particle when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{30}$, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The speed is $|\dot x|$. For $x=a\cos\omega t$, $\dot x=-a\omega\sin\omega t$; the speed is greatest ($a\omega$) when $x=0$ and zero at the ends. Calculator angles in radians.

### Solution

$$\dot x=-0.4(5)\sin5t=-2\sin5t.$$

At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{30}$: $5t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $\dot x=-2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=-1$ and the speed is $1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Check with $v^{2}=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-x^{2})$: $x=0.4\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6}\approx0.346$, $v^{2}=25(0.16-0.12)=1$.

**Answer: b.** The value $0.35$ is the displacement, $1.73$ comes from using $\cos$ instead of $\sin$, and $2$ is the greatest speed.

theme: simple harmonic motion of a particle
enonce_markdown:
A particle moves in simple harmonic motion along a straight line about a fixed point $O$. When the particle is $3\ \mathrm m$ from $O$ its speed is $8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and when it is $4\ \mathrm m$ from $O$ its speed is $6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Find

(i) the angular frequency $\omega$ and the amplitude of the motion,

(ii) the period and the greatest acceleration of the particle,

(iii) the time taken by the particle to travel from $O$ to a point $3\ \mathrm m$ from $O$. *[9 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Use $v^{2}=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-x^{2})$ for the two given positions, and eliminate $a^{2}$ by subtracting. Then $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$, the greatest acceleration is $\omega^{2}a$, and for a particle starting at $O$ the displacement is $x=a\sin\omega t$.

### Solution

**(i)** $64=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-9)$ and $36=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-16)$. Subtracting: $28=7\omega^{2}$, so $\omega^{2}=4$ and $\omega=2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Then $a^{2}-9=16$, so $a^{2}=25$ and the amplitude is $5\ \mathrm m$. (Check: $4(25-16)=36$.)

**(ii)** $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi\ \mathrm s\approx3.14\ \mathrm s$. Greatest acceleration $=\omega^{2}a=4(5)=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

**(iii)** From $O$: $x=5\sin2t=3$, so $\sin2t=0.6$ and

$$t=\frac{\sin^{-1}0.6}{2}\approx\frac{0.6435}{2}\approx0.322\ \mathrm s.$$

theme: simple harmonic motion of a particle
enonce_markdown: A particle moves in simple harmonic motion with period $24\ \mathrm s$ along a line, about a centre $O$, with amplitude $a$. It passes through $O$ at $t=0$. The time taken for it to reach the point whose distance from $O$ is $\tfrac12 a$ for the first time, in seconds, is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Starting from the centre, $x=a\sin\omega t$ with $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$. The motion is not uniform, so the time to cover half the amplitude is not half the time to cover the full amplitude; solve $a\sin\omega t=\tfrac12a$.

### Solution

$\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{24}=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$. Then $\sin\omega t=\tfrac12\Rightarrow\omega t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so

$$t=\frac{\pi/6}{\pi/12}=2\ \mathrm s\qquad\left(=\tfrac{T}{12}\right).$$

**Answer: a.** Option b assumes uniform speed ($T/8$), option c uses $\cos$ in place of $\sin$ ($T/6$), and option d is the time to reach the end of the oscillation ($T/4$).

theme: simple harmonic motion of a particle
enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $0.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ is attached to one end of a light spring of stiffness $8\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, the other end being fixed. The particle oscillates on a smooth horizontal table, the spring remaining taut. The period of the oscillations, in seconds, is
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

By Hooke's law the force on the particle is $-kx$, so $m\ddot x=-kx$, that is $\ddot x=-\dfrac{k}{m}x$. This is simple harmonic motion with $\omega^{2}=\dfrac{k}{m}$ and period $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac mk}$.

### Solution

$$\omega^{2}=\frac{8}{0.5}=16\ \Rightarrow\ \omega=4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},\qquad T=\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}\approx1.57\ \mathrm s.$$

**Answer: b.** Option a uses $\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ (a missing factor $2$), c uses $2\pi\sqrt{mk}$ and d uses $2\pi\sqrt{k/m}$, which inverts the ratio.

theme: simple harmonic motion of a particle
enonce_markdown:
A particle $P$ oscillates in simple harmonic motion along a straight line about a centre $O$, with amplitude $6\ \mathrm m$ and period $4\ \mathrm s$.

(i) Find the angular frequency of the motion and the speed of $P$ when it is $3\ \mathrm m$ from $O$.

(ii) Show that, in each complete oscillation, $P$ is at a distance greater than $3\ \mathrm m$ from $O$ for a total time of $\dfrac83\ \mathrm s$. *[9 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Use $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$ and $v^{2}=\omega^{2}(a^{2}-x^{2})$. For (ii) write the displacement as $x=a\sin\omega t$, solve $|x|>3$ over one cycle, and add the time intervals (or use the symmetry of the motion).

### Solution

**(i)** $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. At $x=3$:

$$v^{2}=\omega^{2}(36-9)=\frac{\pi^{2}}{4}(27)\ \Rightarrow\ v=\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{27}=\frac{3\sqrt3\,\pi}{2}\approx8.16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$

**(ii)** Take $x=6\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2}$. Then $x>3$ when $\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{2}>\tfrac12$, that is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}<\dfrac{\pi t}{2}<\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, so $\tfrac13<t<\tfrac53$: an interval of length $\tfrac43\ \mathrm s$.

By symmetry $x<-3$ for another interval of length $\tfrac43\ \mathrm s$ (in $\tfrac73<t<\tfrac{11}{3}$). Total time per period:

$$\frac43+\frac43=\frac83\ \mathrm s,$$

which is two thirds of the period.
